en: A Verse Summary of the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu*, Volume One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Yijing by Imperial Decree.

Within these miscellaneous matters, there are eight general sections; the grand framework is fully encompassed by one verse for each major section. Within each of these sections, there are further sub-sections, totaling eight verses that summarize them. Within these sub-sections, there are ten verses each, amounting to ninety verses in total. Including the internal summary verses, this reaches approximately one thousand lines.
If one is able to read, recite, and memorize this, one will be thoroughly proficient in its meaning.
The summary verse that encompasses the main sections consists of eight verses in total:
Bricks and stones, as well as cow hair, The three robes, and the senior monk;
The sinews of a fierce beast for Śāriputra; the nun Guptā removes [the hair] from the stūpa.
The summary verse for the first separate section says:
Brick-powder, clipping nails, the bowl, the mirror, the male organ, and treading upon robes.
The water filter, raw beans, and *śu*; the foot-washing cloth should be tied.
A summary verse for the Sub-section on Miscellaneous Items in ten lines:
Brick scrubbers, stones, white earth, ox-gall, incense, and [medicines] that benefit the eyes.
Hitting a pillar and other such conditions—these one should understand as ornaments.
Trimming nails and hair, polishing [the teeth], eating small fruits in the spring;
thirst and the five kinds of medicinal substances—these are explained at length as the conditions for great birth.
One may mend one's bowl and keep necessary requisites:
a knife, a needle-case, and three types of clothing patches; these are permitted by the Great Sage.
One may look at oneself in a mirror or in water, but one should not use combs or brushes.
Leaving long hair on the crown of the head; the *Kṛkī* bathhouse;
protecting the private parts and the face; not engaging in song, dance, or music;
permission for the sound of chanting; and there are four kinds of bowls.
Walking with one's robes and various bags, as well as with mattresses and sitting mats;
when separated from the three robes for a specific reason, there are six kinds of mental recollection rules (*manasikāra-dharma*).
There are five types of water filters (*parisrāvaṇa*), and the sharing of vessels, food, and clothing.
One should know the rules regarding being naked while eating and drinking, and the matter of bathing.
Beans grown in impure ground, spitting, pointing with the finger, and begging;
one should not use copper vessels, though one may keep salt and other such items as needed.
One should provide a place for washing the feet, as well as a basin for rinsing them;
when it is hot, a fan is required, and one should keep five types of whisks ready to ward off mosquitoes and insects.
One should tie the lower robe so it does not rise too high and must not carry heavy burdens.
If one is ill, the use of a staff and a sling is permitted; likewise, the consumption of garlic and other such items is allowed as circumstances dictate.
The summary verse for the second distinct section, consisting of ten topics, says:
Cow-hair [robes], umbrellas, and the occasion of the *pāṃśukūla* (cast-off rags), the wearing of the *saṃkakṣikā*, and the *śrīmatī* (victory-garland) robe.
The renunciant’s medicinal decoction jar, the door leaf, the hammer, and the axe.
A summary verse for the ten items concerning the separate entrance:
"Cow-hair [strainers], and the private parts; sharing a bed, not wearing [the robe] alone;"
If one obtains a white garment, it must be dyed before it may be used.
There is no future life for those who carry parasols; singers do not kindle fires.
When traveling, one seeks a place of reliance; one does not wear a woolen cloak turned inside out.
Regarding the wearing of the *kathina* robe, whether it is permitted or not; one must not set down the bowl when there is an unpleasant sound.
The robe has three types of fastenings, and one should know that the strips [of the inner garment] are likewise three.
Following the matters concerning Śrīmālā and Ajātaśatru, the various necklaces were subsequently prohibited.
Gold bars and colored objects—none of these should be kept.
There are five benefits for those who have left the household life:
not handling money, receiving instruction, the community reciting verses (gāthā), and the permission to use incense tubes and mouthwash.
Medicinal decoctions should be used for bathing; nasal irrigation is performed with a copper cup.
Those who are old or infirm are permitted to use a carriage; one must attend to the matters of excretion and urination.
Knowing the purity or defilement of the water flask, may the World-Honored One enjoy long life.
Because of this, when the nun enters *nirvāṇa*, both chewing and eating are permitted.
Install door panels with keyholes; use leather to pad the area around the central window.
The interior should be wide with latticed doors and pivots; when opening the shop, one must use a "sheep-skin" (latch).
Iron hammers and iron spikes, iron shovels and wooden spades;
five hundred cauldrons, beds, and stoves, as well as axes and chisels, are all permitted.
Saws, axes, and three types of ladders, along with bamboo, wood, and rope, are permitted according to need.
The lower section concerns the method for constructing a monastery and explains the causes and conditions regarding *nātha*.
The summary verse for the third distinct section says:
The three robes and the robe-rack, Building a monastery by a river, and salt.
A towel for wiping the face and a towel for wiping the body; one should keep a seat-cloth and a razor in the monastery.
A summary verse for the section on miscellaneous items consists of ten lines:
the dimensions of the three robes' strips and leaves; the legs of the bed and the duster for sweeping away dust.
In the walking area, one should spread a woolen rug; for the stone barrier, it should be kept ready at the proper time.
As for the clothing rack and the lamp-stand, do not allow insects to damage them.
Open the three-sided hut during the heat; this may be recorded as the practice of Nanda.
Chewing tooth-sticks by the riverbank; Rāhula being sent out of the door;
what is permissible and what is impermissible; the two types of robes that should be provided.
Constructing a monastery and installing eaves-nets; the extensive explanation of the reasons for sweeping the ground.
Seeking the Dharma, two youths were mentioned; during the heat, permission was granted to build a shelter.
Rock salt was placed inside a horn, and medicinal vessels were kept on a woolen rug.
When substituting for one who recites the scriptures, one’s feet should be supported by an object.
The face-cloth is coarse and thin; the spittoon and the body-shield;
the iron trough and the paved floor; the sun-crystal and the washing of clothes.
Wiping the body and treading on the snake’s neck; the stone vessel gives rise to doubt.
There are many kinds of dyed robes; one may use them as one pleases within the monastery.
Regarding the requisites for building a temple, the rules for piercing beds, and the etiquette of prostration;
there is a separate set of garments for shaving the hair, and flower garlands should be hung where one sleeps.
One should provide good seats and beds, scented clay and alms-bowl baskets;
oil vessels and the practice of Dharma-discourse, cloth bags and the carrying of the three cords.
One should also keep a razor, as well as items such as nail clippers.
Supporting the bed and reclining pillows; the use of scented earth according to one's inclination.
The summary verse for the fourth separate section says:
The senior monk (*sthavira*), walls and fences, the occasion of breaking [a rule], and nursing the sick.
Caṇḍāla, pigs, sugarcane, and monasteries; the bowl, reliance, and the method for planting trees.
A summary verse for the subsidiary section contains ten lines:
The Elder speaks in reverse order, or they may proceed together until the end.
Filtering to make non-time [afternoon] gruel; no restriction on the location.
A wall, a fence, and a nun’s shaving tools; not wearing polished or shining robes.
Even if one receives but little, it should be shared equally; one should know the proper ritual for washing and cleaning.
When a robe is torn, it must be sewn; when the Moonlight [Sūtra] was heard, there was an immediate verse.
Regarding the distinctions of reliance, three people sat together to listen.
To nurse the sick, one must avoid natural transgressions (*prakṛti-sāvadya*); when about to receive full ordination, one must not climb a tree.
The king and his ministers did not receive the precepts; their hands were cut off, for they should not have acted thus.
Caṇḍa Sautrāntika used the great robe for a short time;
Śreṣṭha Vasudatta took the bowl with the thought that it was his own property.
Aśvagupta and Candragupta took white robes with the intent of stealing;
this is the same as in the Mahāvinaya, so I shall not trouble to cite it further.
Regarding the pig, sugarcane, and tāla fruit, and the return of the black woolen cloak by Nanda.
One should place knives and needles [in a case], and not use vessels made of lapis lazuli.
One should paint [images] throughout the monastery, as well as maintain lamps and provide facilities for bathing.
One must not step on leaves with alms-bowl water, nor should one eat while wearing shoes.
Ordaining great thieves without a bowl; lacking a preceptor during the rains retreat;
sharing gains for five years; and carrying heavy loads—these should not be done.
Seeking the six requisites through the four reliances; and stealing the robes of a bhikṣu.
The five types of entrustment differ; one must know the rules for dyeing robes.
One must know the rules for planting trees; [the story of] the thief’s cloak and the manifestation of supernatural power.
If one obtains a fine upper robe, one should not cut away the border.
The fifth section, the summary verse, says:
Incineration, interrogation, and the three turnings; Expiation with forfeiture, my own death;
The boundary, and that bhikṣus should not [participate]; The five types of skins are not permitted for use.
The Summary Verse of the Separate Section contains ten lines:
Performing the Threefold Confession while cremating the body; Maudgalyāyana died because he struck [the corpse];
One should not construct it on a large scale; And one must protect many precious treasures.
To interrogate and cause recollection, to ask whether one consents;
not to perform the duties of instruction, the *poṣadha*, or the *pravāraṇā*.
The Buddha turned the Wheel of Dharma three times, first ordaining the five disciples.
One should not address others by name or clan; at Kuśinagara, the concise teaching was proclaimed.
Items subject to forfeiture (nissaggiya-pācittiya) are not to be divided; mosquito nets may be kept as one pleases.
A tripod-shaped vessel should be made like a cauldron; the kaṭhina cloth should be spread.
After death, the entrustment is distinct; if the one to whom it was entrusted dies, the entrustment may be transferred elsewhere.
If the trustee dies, it is entrusted to another person.
One who is outside the boundary does not grant consent (*chanda*); when about to depart, there is no further transmission.
Regarding the matters of the *Poṣadha* and the *Pravāraṇā*: those who violate these will incur transgressions.
Bhikṣus should know the number [of their years]; during the *Pravāraṇā*, they may cast voting sticks as they wish.
One should not sit together with laypeople; seniority among the young and old shall follow the number of years since ordination (*varṣa*).
One should not sit upon stored seats, nor entice others to seek them;
one should not make vows regarding gambling with objects, nor eat the remains left by tigers.
It is improper to hide one's own body, nor to engage in formal announcements and the like.
If one obtains precious jewels of high value, they should be sold and the proceeds shared equally.
Five types of skins should not be used, and the same applies to other similar kinds;
however, when suffering from hemorrhoids, one may wear sandals made of bear skin.
The summary verse for the sixth section says:
Sinews of fierce beasts are not permitted; The lamp-light and the courageous one;
The dharma of crossing with a rope, And because of [the request] granted to Gautamī.
A nun should not precede a layman; she may provide him with other bedding.
It is improper to suddenly splash water; this general summary verse should be understood.
The sub-verse summarizing the ten lines of the specific section follows:
Boots laced with the sinews and hides of fierce beasts, Covering both the front and the back;
Those with two points or a pointed tip— None of these boots are suitable.
When the Four Great Kings were first born, Their radiance shone everywhere in all directions.
Because of these events, his parents each established names for him:
"Guardian in the Womb," because he was protected while in the womb; "Lotus-Step," because upon birth he stepped upon lotus flowers;
"Solely Honored," because as soon as he raised his hands, he was acclaimed supreme; and "Flower-Raiment," because as he was bathed, celestial flowers fell like garments.
Asita beheld the marks; Nālāda urged his teacher.
Five hundred omens appeared before them, and the King, his father, established three names.
He entrusted the Prince to his mother to raise him, commanding her to observe the marks of a Great Man.
Asita traveled from afar and personally beheld the form of the Muni.
Dīpaṃkara became king and possessed five excellent jewels;
because he recounted these wondrous events, he spoke extensively of Gandhāra.
The owl and the crane drink milk; the tips and bases of the *māṅgalya* grass are equal.
The speckled patterns match the fur; the water in the sand-basin does not overflow.
Salt and flour differ from water; the cloth and the tile turn into dust.
This is called Gandhāra; the world considers ten matters.
When Candraprabha personally questioned his mother, he learned that she was born from a scorpion;
he gave her five hundred pieces of gold and drove her out of the country.
Prabhāsa and Upavāna, Kanaka and Jīvaka;
Narada attained the fruit, and Sunakṣatra held oil in his bowl.
On the upper terrace he met Virūḍhaka, and the courtesan observed the stars at night.
Because he made the sound of a horse’s neigh, the merchant carried a dry bone;
Nandipāla the hunter died, and Gopālaka released Tiṣyarakṣitā to return home;
Candraprabha went toward Takṣaśilā, where he killed a man by means of a dream.
Prasenajit was the giver of all; Bimbisāra first renounced his cake.
Anāthapiṇḍada provided bedding and seats; Sudatta built the monastery for the Saṅgha.
When Māndhātṛ died naked, he was not subject to the three kinds of difficulties.
Contemplating without weariness and never sleeping—these seven verses in total summarize it all:
the woodpecker died within the forest; the monkey perished beneath the tree;
in this world and the worlds beyond, one should recognize these four types of blind darkness.
Nakedness is empty and useless; pestle and mortar should be but one.
When affliction gives rise to doubt, matters of contempt must proceed gradually.
There are three kinds of foolish people, and there are three distinctions in causing division.
The lowest grade should be torn apart by chariots; one must recognize the nature of deceitful affairs.
It is difficult to act for the sake of others; solitary matters are mostly hollow.
When actions are contradictory, one should strike heavily; losing one's way brings no benefit.
One should not serve what is improper, nor dwell upon what is unwholesome; one should drive away that which is discordant.
One should abandon fear, lack of joy, and longing;
one should avoid the sorrow of difficult thoughts and insatiable attachment to pleasant things, as well as playing with others and the seizing of wealth.
Not contending with others, no evil intent, No reliance on companions, no lack of faith;
Neither sleep nor desire, The nine afflictions, and no heart of compassion;
The ten evils and their ten opposites— These are manifested by the Ten-Powered One among devas and humans.
The Valiant One and the Precious Vessel; The Wondrous Light in the Āraṇya;
Because he could sustain life, he opened the way for medicine; One who harms the multitude shall not be ordained.
Dhāsa and the other three are the same; Forgetting the origins and asking about them.
The Great Sage of Great Supernatural Power, with his great medicinal herb, cut down from the celestial palace.
He established the Eight Rules of Respect for the ordination of nuns; nuns were to sit according to their seniority.
The affairs of the two divisions differed; those who had returned to lay life were not to be ordained as nuns.
One receives full ordination from bhikṣus; every half-month, one requests instruction from them.
One observes the summer retreat in dependence upon bhikṣus; having seen a fault, one should not speak of it.
One should not scold or revile, nor pay homage to those of lesser standing; with a joyful mind, one remains within the assembly.
One may address a bhikṣu as one pleases; these are known as the eight rules of respect.
Because of the ordination of Gautamī, there are five benefits to renouncing the world.
One should know that within the fivefold assembly, matters of censure are to be understood.
A nun shall not walk ahead; seeing a monk, she should rise in respect.
She may sit on a seat half-reclined before the Saṃgha; if she returns to lay life, there is no cause for reproach.
When an elder offers leftover food, one should not avoid contact with such leftovers.

One should not inquire into private or trivial matters; one should know that when sitting near those who have attained full ordination (*upasampadā*), a bhikṣu’s extra bedding and requisites should be given to a bhikṣuṇī.
A bhikṣuṇī must not step on the planks of a bridge, nor should she wear items intended for personal adornment.
Do not splash water so as to soil one’s robes; do not carry a dead fetus;
do not swallow impurities; and when touching one’s own child, it is not the same as touching another’s.
The summary verse for the seventh separate section says:

Guptā the nun does not remain; saṃkakṣikā, hermaphrodite, narrow path, *karmavācanā*, liquor, changing gender, outside the monastery, and stone. This summary verse of the separate section contains ten lines: The nun Guptā does not remain [in the community];
The *saṃkakṣikā* garment, the hermaphrodite, A narrow path, the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), Liquor, changing one's sexual organs, Outside the monastery, and the stone.
This summary verse of the separate section comprises ten lines:
Guptā slept with her son; the yakṣa deity of Rājagṛha gave the boy a garment to tie around his neck, called him by name, and offered him sacrificial food.
A bhikṣuṇī should not dwell in an araṇya, nor reside in a monastery outside the city.
One must not look out from the doorway, nor show oneself through the window.
It is permitted to wear the saṃkakṣikā; if there are men present, one should not bathe in a pond.
One should not cross at a major intersection, but should instead walk along the side of the road.
If she is a hermaphrodite, or one of the "united-path" class;
or one from whom blood constantly flows, or one who has no blood at all.
If her vaginal opening is small, she should wear inner garments; she must not spit when near a bhikṣu.
The monks and nuns shall not speak face-to-face; it should be done in the presence of their own respective assemblies.
When the bhikṣus perform the *karmavācanā*, the bhikṣuṇīs should listen with focused attention.
They should arrange seats and have people sit down, ensuring that the seats for the nuns are clearly distinguished.
One should not enter taverns or the houses of courtesans; on the road, one must not touch women.
One should adjust one's undergarments according to the occasion, and should not engage in singing or dancing.
If the sexual organs of a monk or nun undergo a transformation, they shall all be expelled after the third occurrence.
Extensively expound the Dharma and its conditions; let the color of a lotus flower serve as the messenger.
Do not perform repentance outside the monastery; do not allow shaving of the hair alone.
Do not rent rooms in a nunnery; do not rub the body with bricks or similar objects.
One should not rub the body with bone or stone, nor with wood or the fist;
one should rub it only with the hand, for no other objects are appropriate.
The summary verse for the eighth section says:
The section on the confession before the stupa, Being appointed [to a task], one should not keep [certain items];
Not associating with women due to a wife; Purgative medicine, the three robes, and snakes.
A summary verse for the sub-sections of this chapter contains ten lines:
Except for repairing damage to a stūpa, Upāli, one must not transgress the monastic regulations;
nuns may enter when there is no obstacle, and they should follow along with the instructions and admonitions.
One must not treat a nun’s confession lightly; if she acts according to her own will, the *poṣadha* (fortnightly confession) shall not be performed.
They should take turns in receiving apologies; it should be known that the nuns sit [for this].
Purification (poṣadha) is not performed at the gate; two nuns must be appointed for this.
When the time for purification arrives, one should appoint someone to wait for the nuns' announcement.
When summoned, one should not avoid going; one should inquire after the name of the preceptor.
Wearing a hat as a bowl-sack is improper; it is not fitting for a *bhikṣuṇī* to tie flower garlands.
One should not keep copper vessels; fermented liquor should be transformed and restored to its original state.
Do not rent rooms to lay travelers; do not practice medicine or sorcery out of deception.
Do not bathe with women, nor wash against the current of a river.
One should place a mat beneath the bowl and must not keep glass cups.
The staff is regulated by the rules for women; dancing while rising incurs an offense.
Accepting moist cakes as an invitation to eat, preaching the Dharma, and informing one's companion.
Laxatives, poison on the teeth, and the tongue-scraper must be washed.
Through the exhaustion of their karmic offenses, they realized arhatship.
One should wear the three robes according to the occasion; know that this is the dharma for forest hermits (araṇyaka).
Guarding the bathhouse, keeping watch at the gate, and [offering] exquisite flowers—these are not places where one should dwell.
One should inspect bedding for snakes; a single robe does not constitute a formal salutation.
When first arriving at a monastery, one should perform four prostrations to those of seniority.
The World-Honored One, being supreme and exalted, has extensively expounded the conduct of disciples.
Vassakāra questioned the Great Master, who then expounded the seven and six dharmas.
The assembly gathered and revered the Great Master; hearing the Dharma, they gave rise to right faith.
[The Master] recounted his own advanced age and explained the causal conditions for Vassakāra.
Vassakāra dwelt within the Bamboo Grove, while Paṭaligāma was being fortified;
crossing the river, he went to the small tree, gradually approaching Nirvāṇa and other matters.
In the thirty-seventh fascicle, the four black and white [omens] are recorded, followed by the account of the events of the Parinirvāṇa.
The thirty-eighth [chapter] describes how the non-Buddhist ascetic Bhadra attained the fruit [of arhatship], followed by an account of the various kingdoms contending for the relics.
The thirty-ninth [chapter] describes the Brahmin distributing the relics among the various kingdoms, as well as the council convened by Gavāmpati, and so forth.
The fortieth [chapter], describing the events of the Councils of Five Hundred and Seven Hundred Monks.
A Summary Verse from the *Vinayakṣudrakavastu* of the Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya, one fascicle.
Translated on the fifteenth day (the Jingshen day) of the fourth month in the year of Gengxu during the Jinglong era of the Great Tang. By the Tripiṭaka Master.
The Dharma Master, the Venerable Yijing, proclaimed and explained the Indic original, compiled the prose, and corrected the orthography;
the Sramana from Tukhara, the Venerable Dharmasoma, verified the Indic meaning; the Sramana from Central India, the Venerable Banu, verified the Indic meaning;
and the Sramana from Kaśmīra, the Venerable Dharmānanda, verified [the Indic meaning].
Śramaṇa-translator of the Sanskrit scriptures, Venerable Huizhao of Dayun Monastery in Zizhou;
Śramaṇa-translator of the scriptures, Venerable Vinaya Master Daolin of Chongxian Monastery in Luozhou, who verified the meaning;
Śramaṇa-translator, Venerable Dailiang, Abbot of Fushou Monastery, who verified the meaning; and Śramaṇa-translator, Venerable [Name] of Taiping Monastery in Luozhou.
Dharma Master Daoke served as the *sākṣin* (witness/verifier) for the meaning; the śramaṇa of the Great Jianfu Monastery, the Venerable Shengzhuang, served as the *sākṣin* for the meaning;

the śramaṇa of Xiangzhou’s Shanhe Monastery, the Venerable Xuansan, served as the *sākṣin* for the meaning; the śramaṇa of the Great Jianfu Monastery, the Venerable Vinaya Master Zhiji, served as the scribe (*lekhaka*) for the translation;
and [the Venerable] served as the corrector of the orthography (*saṃśodhaka*).
Sramana Hui-san, Abbot of Dayun Monastery in Dezhou, verified the meaning;
Sramana Hui-ji, Virtuous One of Botai Monastery in Xiliangzhou, read the Sanskrit manuscript;

and the Brahmin translator, Minister Gu Jin-gang—appointed as an Extraordinary Official of the Left Garrison Command of the Eastern Indian Kingdom and serving concurrently as a Middle General of the Auxiliary Bureau—verified [the translation].
The Brahmin translator of the scriptures, the Great Chief Minister of East India, Īśvara;
the Brahmin translator of the scriptures who served as witness, the General of the Left Guard of the Central Cavalry, Prince of Kaśmīra, the Subject Aśuna;
and the Brahmin translator of the scriptures, the Left Spear-Bearer of East India, serving in the Secretariat of the Central Secretariat.
I, the subject Du, who has read the Sanskrit manuscripts with some proficiency, together with the Brahmin translator of scriptures from the great officialdom of the country of Longbo (Lombok),
who ranks as a fifth-grade official, Li Shuluo; the witness-translator, the Golden Light Luofu Dafa, Acting Minister of the Left of the Department of State Affairs,
concurrently holding the rank of Third Grade of the Secretariat and Chancellery, Upper Pillar of State, Duke of Shu, the subject Wei Wuyuan, and others.
The thirty-three scholars of the Xiuwen Pavilion, together with the Supervising Official and Court Rank San-si-da-fu,

Acting Assistant Director of the Bureau of Literary Composition, Your Majesty’s Subject Liu Lingzhi; and the Envoy, Imperially Invested Jin-zi-guang-lu-dafu, Director of the Secretariat, Acting Inspector of the Palace Attendants,
concurrently in charge of the Inner and Outer Stables and the Three Commissions of Longyou, Grand Marshal and Successor to the Title, Your Majesty’s Subject Wang Yong.
